H&P – Super Detailed Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
27-year-old male with 3-day history of profuse hourly watery diarrhoea, crampy mid-lower abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting (milk-triggered), and subjective fever—most consistent with acute infective gastroenteritis; conservative outpatient management with oral rehydration solution, soft diet, paracetamol, and 48-hour safety-net advice given.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “very watery diarrhoea” for 3 days.  
• Onset/Timeline – Began Monday/Tuesday (≈3 days ago); persists with no improvement.  
• Frequency/Quantity – Bowel movements almost every hour while awake; described as “just fluids” with no formed stool.  
• Stool characteristics – Watery; denies blood or mucus.  
• Abdominal pain – Crampy, mid-lower abdomen, colicky, precedes stool passage, intensity ~6/10, intermittent.  
• Nausea/Vomiting – Present; occasional emesis, particularly after milk ingestion.  
• Subjective fever/“burning up” – Feels hot; no temperature recorded.  
• Urinary output – Passing urine, though feels less frequent.  
• Oral intake – Drinks water/fluids but feels it “goes straight through.” Able to take some solid food (lunch) but stools remain loose.  
• Exposures – Brother had similar illness x5 days (now improving); no recent travel stated.  
• Review of systems (limited) – No bleeding per rectum, no weight loss, no chronic GI symptoms, no respiratory or urinary pain reported.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported; “otherwise fit and well.”  
• No prior gastrointestinal disease documented.  

Medications:
• Paracetamol – dose/route/frequency not documented (used for pain/fever).  
• No regular prescribed medications.

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives with mother and sister; brother lives separately.  
• Employment: Government office worker in Central London.  
• Smoking: Social smoker (occasional cigarettes on weekends).  
• Alcohol: Moderate beer intake on weekdays; binge drinking once or twice per month.  
• Diet: Frequently purchases takeaway food; rarely eats family meals.  

Family History:
• Father – Stage III colon cancer (current).  
• Brother – Current self-limited diarrhoeal illness (≈5 days).  
• No known family history of inflammatory bowel disease.

Physical Examination:
(No in-person exam; teleconsultation)  
• Vitals: Not measured.  
• General appearance: Not documented beyond video link.

Investigations:
• None performed or available at time of consult.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute watery diarrhoea, likely viral gastroenteritis  
  • Assessment: Sudden onset, high frequency watery stools, associated nausea/vomiting, subjective fever, household contact with similar illness, no red-flag features (no blood, severe pain, or immunosuppression).  
  • Plan:  
    – Oral rehydration therapy: Purchase over-the-counter Dioralyte; use as directed.  
    – Hydration: Encourage clear fluids; avoid alcohol and caffeine.  
    – Diet: Begin with clear fluids → soft/bland diet (soups, mashed foods) as tolerated; avoid dairy temporarily.  
    – Symptomatic relief: Continue paracetamol for pain/fever (dose not documented).  
    – Safety-net: If symptoms worsen, inability to keep fluids down, signs of dehydration, or no improvement in 48 hours, contact clinician for review ± further investigations (stool cultures, blood tests, IV fluids).  

Issue 2 – Risk of dehydration  
  • Assessment: Hourly watery stools, subjective reduced urine frequency.  
  • Plan: Emphasise strict oral rehydration; monitor urine output & mental status; early follow-up if worsening.

Issue 3 – Family history of colorectal cancer  
  • Assessment: Father with stage III colon cancer; current presentation appears infectious rather than neoplastic, but family risk noted.  
  • Plan: Document family history; routine colorectal cancer screening discussion at appropriate age (not acute priority).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis (norovirus) – High likelihood: abrupt onset, profuse watery diarrhoea, household contact, short course typical.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/food-borne infection – Moderate likelihood: takeaway food habit, subjective fever; lacks bloody stools.  
3. Transient post-infectious lactose intolerance – Low-moderate likelihood: milk provokes vomiting; may contribute to symptoms but not primary cause.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: No objective vitals (temperature, BP, HR), no formal physical exam, no medication doses, allergies reviewed but limited.  
• Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor conversational pauses but clinically adequate.
